claim: The neuronal microtubule cytoskeleton underlies the polarization and proper functioning of neurons by providing tracks for motor proteins that drive intracellular transport.
source: The neuronal microtubule cytoskeleton underlies the polarization and proper functioning of neurons, amongst others by providing tracks for motor proteins that drive intracellular transport.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general background claim about neuronal microtubule function.

claim: Different subsets of neuronal microtubules varying in composition, stability, and motor preference exist.
source: Different subsets of neuronal microtubules, varying in composition, stability, and motor preference, are known to exist, but the high density of microtubules has so far precluded mapping their relative abundance and three-dimensional organization.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and references existing knowledge in the field.

claim: The high density of microtubules has precluded mapping their relative abundance and three-dimensional organization.
source: Different subsets of neuronal microtubules, varying in composition, stability, and motor preference, are known to exist, but the high density of microtubules has so far precluded mapping their relative abundance and three-dimensional organization.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous research in the abstract.

claim: In dendrites, acetylated microtubules are enriched in the core of the dendritic shaft.
source: This revealed that in dendrites acetylated microtubules are enriched in the core of the dendritic shaft, while tyrosinated microtubules are enriched near the plasma membrane, thus forming a shell around the acetylated microtubules.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: Tyrosinated microtubules are enriched near the plasma membrane in dendrites, forming a shell around the acetylated microtubules.
source: This revealed that in dendrites acetylated microtubules are enriched in the core of the dendritic shaft, while tyrosinated microtubules are enriched near the plasma membrane, thus forming a shell around the acetylated microtubules.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: Acetylated microtubules account for 65-75% of all microtubules in dendrites.
source: Moreover, using a novel analysis pipeline we quantified the absolute number of acetylated and tyrosinated microtubules within dendrites and found that they account for 65–75% and ~20–30% of all microtubules, respectively, leaving only few microtubules that do not fall in either category.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Tyrosinated microtubules account for approximately 20-30% of all microtubules in dendrites.
source: Moreover, using a novel analysis pipeline we quantified the absolute number of acetylated and tyrosinated microtubules within dendrites and found that they account for 65–75% and ~20–30% of all microtubules, respectively, leaving only few microtubules that do not fall in either category.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Only few microtubules in dendrites do not fall into either the acetylated or tyrosinated category.
source: Moreover, using a novel analysis pipeline we quantified the absolute number of acetylated and tyrosinated microtubules within dendrites and found that they account for 65–75% and ~20–30% of all microtubules, respectively, leaving only few microtubules that do not fall in either category.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Different microtubule subtypes facilitate different motor proteins.
source: Because these different microtubule subtypes facilitate different motor proteins, these novel insights help to understand the spatial regulation of intracellular transport.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The extended and polarized morphology of neurons is established and maintained by the cytoskeleton.
source: The extended and polarized morphology of neurons is established and maintained by the cytoskeleton (Stiess and Bradke, 2011; Bentley and Banker, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The microtubule cytoskeleton provides a transport network inside the neuron's long axon and branched dendrites.
source: One of the functions of the microtubule cytoskeleton is to provide a transport network inside the neurons long axon and branched dendrites (Kapitein and Hoogenraad, 2015; Burute and Kapitein, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Directional transport is enabled by the structural polarity of microtubules, which is recognized by motor proteins.
source: Directional transport is enabled by the structural polarity of microtubules, which is recognized by motor proteins that drive transport to either the minus end (dynein) or plus end (most kinesins).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Dynein drives transport to the minus end of microtubules.
source: Directional transport is enabled by the structural polarity of microtubules, which is recognized by motor proteins that drive transport to either the minus end (dynein) or plus end (most kinesins).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Most kinesins drive transport to the plus end of microtubules.
source: Directional transport is enabled by the structural polarity of microtubules, which is recognized by motor proteins that drive transport to either the minus end (dynein) or plus end (most kinesins).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: The affinity of motors for the microtubule lattice can be modulated by microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs).
source: Previous work has revealed that the affinity of motors for the microtubule lattice can be modulated by microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) or by post-translational modifications (PTMs) of tubulin (Atherton et al., 2013; Sirajuddin et al., 2014; Jurriens et al., 2021; Monroy et al., 2020; Park and Roll-Mecak, 2018; Janke and Magiera, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The affinity of motors for the microtubule lattice can be modulated by post-translational modifications (PTMs) of tubulin.
source: Previous work has revealed that the affinity of motors for the microtubule lattice can be modulated by microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) or by post-translational modifications (PTMs) of tubulin (Atherton et al., 2013; Sirajuddin et al., 2014; Jurriens et al., 2021; Monroy et al., 2020; Park and Roll-Mecak, 2018; Janke and Magiera, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Kinesin-1 motors move preferentially on microtubules marked by acetylation and detyrosination.
source: For example, kinesin-1 motors move preferentially on microtubules marked by acetylation and detyrosination (Cai et al., 2009; Dunn et al., 2008), while kinesin-3 prefers tyrosinated microtubules (Guardia et al., 2016; Tas et al., 2017; Lipka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Kinesin-3 prefers tyrosinated microtubules.
source: For example, kinesin-1 motors move preferentially on microtubules marked by acetylation and detyrosination (Cai et al., 2009; Dunn et al., 2008), while kinesin-3 prefers tyrosinated microtubules (Guardia et al., 2016; Tas et al., 2017; Lipka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: When tubulin is incorporated into the microtubule lattice, it carries a genetically encoded C-terminal tyrosine.
source: When tubulin is incorporated into the microtubule lattice, it carries a genetically encoded C-terminal tyrosine, which can subsequently be proteolytically removed to yield detyrosinated microtubules (Kapitein and Hoogenraad, 2015; Janke and Magiera, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The C-terminal tyrosine can be proteolytically removed to yield detyrosinated microtubules.
source: When tubulin is incorporated into the microtubule lattice, it carries a genetically encoded C-terminal tyrosine, which can subsequently be proteolytically removed to yield detyrosinated microtubules (Kapitein and Hoogenraad, 2015; Janke and Magiera, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Tyrosinated tubulin can be regarded as a marker for freshly polymerized microtubules.
source: Therefore, tyrosinated tubulin can be regarded as a marker for freshly polymerized microtubules.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from the previous statement about tyrosination.

claim: Freshly polymerized microtubules undergo cycles of growth and shrinkage and are referred to as dynamic microtubules.
source: Such microtubules undergo cycles of growth and shrinkage and are therefore referred to as dynamic microtubules.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Following polymerization, tubulins can acquire new chemical groups through post-translational modifications, such as acetylation and polyglutamylation.
source: Following polymerization, tubulins can also acquire new chemical groups through post-translational modifications, such as acetylation and polyglutamylation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Detyrosinated tubulin can be further proteolytically processed at the C-terminal to yield delta 2-tubulin.
source: Additionally, detyrosinated tubulin can be further proteolytically processed at the C-terminal to yield delta 2-tubulin (Paturle-Lafanechère et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Post-translational modifications often accumulate on microtubules that are long-lived and resist cold-induced or drug-induced depolymerization.
source: Such modifications often accumulate on microtubules that are long-lived and resist cold-induced or drug-induced depolymerization, which are therefore termed stable microtubules.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Microtubules that are long-lived and resist depolymerization are termed stable microtubules.
source: Such modifications often accumulate on microtubules that are long-lived and resist cold-induced or drug-induced depolymerization, which are therefore termed stable microtubules.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Little is known about the relative abundance and spatial organization of different microtubule subsets within neurons.
source: Despite many biochemical and physiological studies underpinning the importance of various microtubule modifications (Sirajuddin et al., 2014; Janke and Magiera, 2020; Nekooki-Machida and Hagiwara, 2020; Roll-Mecak, 2019), little is known about the relative abundance and spatial organization of different microtubule subsets within neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Stable and dynamic microtubules in dendrites are organized differently and often have opposite orientations.
source: In earlier work, we revealed that stable and dynamic microtubules in dendrites are organized differently and often have opposite orientations, explaining why kinesin-3 can drive efficient anterograde transport in dendrites, unlike kinesin-1 (Tas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: The opposite orientations of stable and dynamic microtubules explain why kinesin-3 can drive efficient anterograde transport in dendrites, unlike kinesin-1.
source: In earlier work, we revealed that stable and dynamic microtubules in dendrites are organized differently and often have opposite orientations, explaining why kinesin-3 can drive efficient anterograde transport in dendrites, unlike kinesin-1 (Tas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: Electron microscopy has been used to reveal the number and spatial organization of microtubules in dendrite cross-sections.
source: Although microtubule organization in dendrites has previously been studied using electron microscopy (Baas et al., 1988; Kubota et al., 2011), this method is difficult to combine with selective markers and therefore cannot robustly identify and map microtubule subsets throughout dendrites.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Electron microscopy is difficult to combine with selective markers and cannot robustly identify and map microtubule subsets throughout dendrites.
source: Although microtubule organization in dendrites has previously been studied using electron microscopy (Baas et al., 1988; Kubota et al., 2011), this method is difficult to combine with selective markers and therefore cannot robustly identify and map microtubule subsets throughout dendrites.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of electron microscopy.

claim: The intensity of both total tubulin and acetylated and tyrosinated subsets decreased as the dendrite became smaller, displaying a quadratic dependence on dendrite width.
source: Whereas the intensity of both total tubulin and these two subsets decreased as the dendrite became smaller (displaying a quadratic dependence on dendrite width), the relative intensity of both subsets was nearly constant along the dendrite (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The relative intensity of acetylated and tyrosinated subsets was nearly constant along the dendrite.
source: Whereas the intensity of both total tubulin and these two subsets decreased as the dendrite became smaller (displaying a quadratic dependence on dendrite width), the relative intensity of both subsets was nearly constant along the dendrite (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The antibody used for detyrosinated tubulin did not obtain reliable staining in neurons.
source: However, whereas the antibody that we used did reveal clear overlap between acetylation and detyrosination in non-neuronal cells, we did not obtain reliable staining in neurons, (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Delta 2-tubulin was found on a subset of microtubules that overlapped with the most central part of the acetylated bundles.
source: Delta 2-tubulin was found on a subset of microtubules that overlapped with the most central part of the acetylated bundles, but was not further explored here (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Individual microtubules could not be distinguished within axons or dendrites using STED microscopy.
source: However, we were unable to distinguish individual microtubules within axons or dendrites, since (as it is known from electron microscopy studies) the distance between adjacent microtubules is often smaller than the resolution of STED (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Baas et al., 1988; Baas et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to electron microscopy studies.

claim: The distance between adjacent microtubules in axons or dendrites is often smaller than the resolution of STED.
source: However, we were unable to distinguish individual microtubules within axons or dendrites, since (as it is known from electron microscopy studies) the distance between adjacent microtubules is often smaller than the resolution of STED (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Baas et al., 1988; Baas et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to electron microscopy studies.

claim: Microtubules in the cell body were more dispersed and individual microtubules could often be resolved.
source: Microtubules in the cell body, however, were more dispersed and here individual microtubules could often be resolved (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Segments detected by acetylation have, on average, lower levels of tyrosination than segments detected by tyrosination.
source: The resulting histograms show that segments detected by acetylation have, on average, lower levels of tyrosination than segments detected by tyrosination, and vice versa (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Segments detected by tyrosination have, on average, lower levels of acetylation than segments detected by acetylation.
source: The resulting histograms show that segments detected by acetylation have, on average, lower levels of tyrosination than segments detected by tyrosination, and vice versa (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Acetylation and tyrosination mark two different subsets of microtubules.
source: This quantitatively confirms the general impression that these chemical groups mark two different subsets and that microtubules with high levels of acetylation are mostly detyrosinated.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data analysis.

claim: Microtubules with high levels of acetylation are mostly detyrosinated.
source: This quantitatively confirms the general impression that these chemical groups mark two different subsets and that microtubules with high levels of acetylation are mostly detyrosinated.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data analysis.

claim: Highly acetylated microtubules display residual tyrosination.
source: However, despite clearly separating into two subsets, even highly acetylated microtubules display residual tyrosination, whereas many tyrosinated microtubules have some extent of acetylation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: Many tyrosinated microtubules have some extent of acetylation.
source: However, despite clearly separating into two subsets, even highly acetylated microtubules display residual tyrosination, whereas many tyrosinated microtubules have some extent of acetylation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: The measured relative level of tyrosination for acetylated microtubules (α) was equal to 0.53 ± 0.11.
source: The measured relative level of tyrosination for acetylated microtubules, compared to average tyrosination of tyrosinated microtubules, which we termed α, was equal to 0.53 ± 0.11 (average ± SD) and the level of acetylation for tyrosinated microtubules, compared to the acetylation of acetylated microtubules, termed β, was 0.45 ± 0.07 (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The level of acetylation for tyrosinated microtubules (β) was 0.45 ± 0.07.
source: The measured relative level of tyrosination for acetylated microtubules, compared to average tyrosination of tyrosinated microtubules, which we termed α, was equal to 0.53 ± 0.11 (average ± SD) and the level of acetylation for tyrosinated microtubules, compared to the acetylation of acetylated microtubules, termed β, was 0.45 ± 0.07 (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Microtubules detected in the acetylated tubulin channel display on average 47% lower levels of tyrosination than microtubules detected in the tyrosinated channel.
source: We will refer to microtubules detected in the acetylated tubulin channel, displaying on average 47% lower levels of tyrosination than microtubules detected in the tyrosinated channel, as stable microtubules.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a definition based on the data.

claim: Dynamic microtubules feature 55% lower levels of acetylation than microtubules detected in the acetylated channel.
source: Likewise, dynamic microtubules are identified as microtubules detected in the tyrosinated tubulin channel and feature 55% lower levels of acetylation than microtubules detected in the acetylated channel.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a definition based on the data.

claim: The total number of microtubules in a dendrite depends linearly on its cross-sectional area in the range from 1 to 10 μm2 with a slope of 68 microtubules per μm2.
source: First of all, this showed that the total number of microtubules in a dendrite depends linearly on its cross-sectional area in the range from 1 to 10 μm2 with a slope of 68 microtubules per μm2.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the Results section based on STED data.

claim: Dendrites have over four times more acetylated microtubules than tyrosinated microtubules (74 ± 8% versus 16 ± 11%).
source: In addition, it revealed that dendrites have over four times more acetylated microtubules than tyrosinated microtubules (74 ± 8% versus 16 ± 11%, average ± SD) and that this factor was largely independent of the diameter of the dendrite (Figure 3C,D,E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The ratio of acetylated to tyrosinated microtubules is largely independent of the diameter of the dendrite.
source: In addition, it revealed that dendrites have over four times more acetylated microtubules than tyrosinated microtubules (74 ± 8% versus 16 ± 11%, average ± SD) and that this factor was largely independent of the diameter of the dendrite (Figure 3C,D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: A small fraction of 10 ± 14% of microtubules were classified as neither acetylated nor tyrosinated.
source: We furthermore found that these two subsets did not completely account for the total number of microtubules that we measured, leaving a small fraction of 10 ± 14% of microtubules that were classified as neither acetylated nor tyrosinated.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the Results section based on STED data.

claim: Expanded samples demonstrated a substantial increase in the clarity with which microtubule organization could be perceived.
source: Indeed, expanded samples demonstrated a substantial increase in the clarity with which microtubule organization could be perceived (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The peripheral enrichment of tyrosinated microtubules was even more pronounced in ExM samples.
source: We therefore repeated our analysis of the spatial distribution of tyrosinated and acetylated microtubules and found that the peripheral enrichment of tyrosinated microtubules was even more pronounced in ExM samples, as shown in y,z cross-section images (Figure 4B) and radial distribution plots (Figure 4C,D,E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Decomposition of the radial density of total tubulin as a sum of acetylated and tyrosinated radial densities confirms the prevalence of acetylated microtubules (65%) over tyrosinated (35%).
source: Although this analysis does not take into account the fraction of microtubules that is neither tyrosinated or acetylated, it independently confirms the prevalence of acetylated microtubules (65%) over tyrosinated (35%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from ExM data analysis.

claim: The average tyrosination level of acetylated microtubules measured using FlipExM was 0.45 ± 0.05.
source: Compared to the cell body data, we found slightly different values for the average tyrosination level of acetylated microtubules (0.45 ± 0.05), as well as the acetylation level for tyrosinated microtubules (0.60 ± 0.17) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The acetylation level for tyrosinated microtubules measured using FlipExM was 0.60 ± 0.17.
source: Compared to the cell body data, we found slightly different values for the average tyrosination level of acetylated microtubules (0.45 ± 0.05), as well as the acetylation level for tyrosinated microtubules (0.60 ± 0.17) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: A linear fit through the total number of microtubules as a function of cross-sectional area yields an estimated microtubule density of 68 microtubules per square micrometer for the cell body method.
source: A linear fit through the total number of microtubules as a function of cross-sectional area yields an estimated microtubule density of 68 and 53 microtubules per square micrometer for the cell body and dendrite methods, respectively (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5J.

claim: A linear fit through the total number of microtubules as a function of cross-sectional area yields an estimated microtubule density of 53 microtubules per square micrometer for the dendrite method.
source: A linear fit through the total number of microtubules as a function of cross-sectional area yields an estimated microtubule density of 68 and 53 microtubules per square micrometer for the cell body and dendrite methods, respectively (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Stable, acetylated microtubules form the largest population at 72 ± 6%.
source: Consistent with our earlier results, this analysis revealed that stable, acetylated microtubules form the largest population (72 ± 6%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the Results section based on FlipExM data.

claim: The fraction of tyrosinated microtubules measured using FlipExM was 26 ± 8%.
source: The fraction of tyrosinated microtubules was larger than our earlier estimate (26 ± 8%), at the expense of the fraction of microtubules that were neither acetylated nor tyrosinated (2 ± 5%, Figure 5H,I, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The fraction of microtubules that were neither acetylated nor tyrosinated measured using FlipExM was 2 ± 5%.
source: The fraction of tyrosinated microtubules was larger than our earlier estimate (26 ± 8%), at the expense of the fraction of microtubules that were neither acetylated nor tyrosinated (2 ± 5%, Figure 5H,I, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Acetylated and tyrosinated microtubules together account for 98% of all dendritic microtubules.
source: These results indicate that acetylated and tyrosinated microtubules together account for 98% of all dendritic microtubules, with acetylated microtubules being almost three times more abundant.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the FlipExM data.

claim: Acetylated microtubules are almost three times more abundant than tyrosinated microtubules.
source: These results indicate that acetylated and tyrosinated microtubules together account for 98% of all dendritic microtubules, with acetylated microtubules being almost three times more abundant.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the FlipExM data.

claim: The high density of the neuronal microtubule cytoskeleton has obscured its exact composition and organization.
source: The high density of the neuronal microtubule cytoskeleton has so far obscured its exact composition and organization.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the problem addressed by the study.

claim: Early work on axonal microtubules successfully detected modified microtubules using immunoelectron microscopy.
source: While early work on axonal microtubules successfully detected modified microtubules using immunoelectron microscopy, these methods have not been systematically applied to dendrites (Baas and Black, 1990; Ahmad et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Immunoelectron microscopy methods have not been systematically applied to dendrites.
source: While early work on axonal microtubules successfully detected modified microtubules using immunoelectron microscopy, these methods have not been systematically applied to dendrites (Baas and Black, 1990; Ahmad et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Volumetric STED and expansion microscopy revealed a striking spatial organization in which stable, acetylated microtubules are enriched in the core of the dendritic shaft, surrounded by a shell of dynamic, tyrosinated microtubules.
source: Volumetric STED and expansion microscopy revealed a striking spatial organization in which stable, acetylated microtubules are enriched in the core of the dendritic shaft, surrounded by a shell of dynamic, tyrosinated microtubules (Figures 1 and 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the main findings.

claim: The enrichment of dynamic microtubules near the plasma membrane is consistent with the well-established interplay between growing microtubule plus ends and (sub)cortical complexes.
source: The enrichment of dynamic microtubules near the plasma membrane is consistent with the well-established interplay between growing microtubule plus ends and (sub)cortical complexes (van de Willige et al., 2016; Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Dynamic microtubules regularly invade into dendritic spines to facilitate intracellular transport or regulate spine morphology in response to specific synaptic stimuli.
source: More specifically, dynamic microtubules have been shown to regularly invade into dendritic spines to facilitate intracellular transport or regulate spine morphology in response of specific synaptic stimuli (Esteves da Silva et al., 2015; Jaworski et al., 2009; McVicker et al., 2016; Hu et al., 2008; Schätzle et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Spatial separation between stable and dynamic microtubules might promote efficient intracellular transport by separating cargoes driven by subset-specific motors.
source: Next to ensuring the enrichment of dynamic microtubules near the plasma membrane, spatial separation between stable and dynamic microtubules might also promote efficient intracellular transport by separating cargoes driven by subset-specific motors.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation about the functional implications.

claim: For motors that do not discriminate between microtubule subsets, the spatial separation between mostly minus-end out oriented stable microtubules and mostly plus-end out oriented dynamic microtubules will facilitate directional transport by limiting directional switching.
source: Moreover, for motors that do not discriminate between microtubule subsets, the spatial separation between mostly minus-end out oriented stable microtubules and mostly plus-end out oriented dynamic microtubules (Tas et al., 2017) will facilitate directional transport by limiting directional switching induced by cargo-attached motors binding to neighboring microtubules of opposite polarity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation about the functional implications with a supporting citation.

claim: The estimates for the total microtubules (68 or 53 microtubules per μm2) are consistent with earlier estimates using electron microscopy (66 microtubules per μm2).
source: These values are consistent with earlier estimates using electron microscopy (66 microtubules per μm2)(Kubota et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Occasional inclusion of small microtubule bundles could have increased the estimate for single microtubules, thereby lowering the estimate for the total number of microtubules.
source: Although we used various filtering steps to prevent mistaking small microtubule bundles for individual microtubules, it remains possible that occasional inclusion of such bundles increased our estimate for single microtubules, thereby lowering our estimate for the total number of microtubules.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a potential limitation of the method.

claim: The two single-microtubule calibration methods (soma versus dendrite) yielded strikingly similar estimates for the percentage of acetylated microtubules (74 ± 8% versus 72 ± 6%).
source: The two single-microtubule calibration methods (i.e. soma versus dendrite) yielded strikingly similar estimates for the percentage of acetylated microtubules (74 ± 8% versus 72 ± 6%), while their estimates for tyrosinated and other (non-tyrosinated and non-acetylated) microtubules differed to some extent (16% tyrosinated and 10% other microtubules for soma versus 26% and 2% for dendrite estimations, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a comparison of the two methods.

claim: The acetylation level of stable microtubules is similar between soma and dendrites.
source: These results suggest that the acetylation level of stable microtubules is similar between soma and dendrites, whereas the tyrosination level of dynamic microtubules could be higher in the soma than the dendrite.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the data comparison.

claim: The tyrosination level of dynamic microtubules could be higher in the soma than the dendrite.
source: These results suggest that the acetylation level of stable microtubules is similar between soma and dendrites, whereas the tyrosination level of dynamic microtubules could be higher in the soma than the dendrite.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation based on the data comparison.

claim: Dendritic dynamic microtubules are on average more detyrosinated than somatic dynamic microtubules.
source: The idea that dendritic dynamic microtubules are on average more detyrosinated is consistent with our finding that these microtubules also have higher levels of acetylation compared to the soma (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The dendrite-intrinsic measurements are more reliable, yielding 72 ± 6% acetylated, 26 ± 8% tyrosinated and 2 ± 5% other microtubules.
source: We therefore consider the dendrite-intrinsic measurements to be more reliable, that is 72 ± 6% acetylated, 26 ± 8% tyrosinated and 2 ± 5% other microtubules.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as the authors' conclusion about which method is more reliable.

claim: Acetylation and tyrosination represent only a small part of the possible ways in which the microtubule surface can become differentiated.
source: It is important to note that the two markers that we used, acetylation and tyrosination, represent only a small part of the possibly ways in which the microtubule surface can become differentiated, such as through other modifications like polyglutamylation, phosphorylation, palmitoylation, incorporation of different tubulin isoforms, and adsorption of different MAPs (Sirajuddin et al., 2014; Janke and Magiera, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The focus on acetylation and tyrosination was because these modifications label clearly distinct subsets and display the most direct correlation with microtubule stability and motor selectivity.
source: We focused on acetylation and tyrosination because these modifications label clearly distinct subsets and display the most direct correlation with microtubule stability (e.g. only acetylated microtubules remain after nocodazole treatment (Tas et al., 2017) and motor selectivity (e.g. Kinesin-1 binding correlates with acetylation (Tas et al., 2017; Jansen et al., 2021)).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Only acetylated microtubules remain after nocodazole treatment.
source: We focused on acetylation and tyrosination because these modifications label clearly distinct subsets and display the most direct correlation with microtubule stability (e.g. only acetylated microtubules remain after nocodazole treatment (Tas et al., 2017) and motor selectivity (e.g. Kinesin-1 binding correlates with acetylation (Tas et al., 2017; Jansen et al., 2021)).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Kinesin-1 binding correlates with acetylation.
source: We focused on acetylation and tyrosination because these modifications label clearly distinct subsets and display the most direct correlation with microtubule stability (e.g. only acetylated microtubules remain after nocodazole treatment (Tas et al., 2017) and motor selectivity (e.g. Kinesin-1 binding correlates with acetylation (Tas et al., 2017; Jansen et al., 2021)).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The binary classification scheme used to classify microtubules as either acetylated or tyrosinated is most likely an oversimplification.
source: Importantly, the binary classification scheme used to classify microtubules as either acetylated or tyrosinated is most likely an oversimplification that does not do full justice to the rich modification landscape of microtubules, where also different parts of a microtubule can display different modifications (Baas and Black, 1990; Ahmad et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Dissociated hippocampal neuron cultures were prepared from embryonic day 18 rat pups.
source: Dissociated hippocampal neuron cultures were prepared from embryonic day 18 rat pups of mixed gender according to the previously published protocol (Kapitein et al., 2010).

claim: Cells were plated at a density of 50 k/well.
source: Briefly, cells were plated on 18‐mm glass coverslips coated with poly‐l‐lysine (37.5 mg/ml) and laminin (1.25 mg/ml) in a 12‐well plate at a density of 50 k/well.

claim: At DIV9 neurons were pre-extracted for 1 min using 0.3% Triton X-100 and 0.1% glutaraldehyde in MRB80 buffer.
